Apprenticeship Relevance
Breaking down the mission statement for my role is an excellent way to explain how important data
analysis is to my day-to-day tasks:
"Pre-empting and solving underlying product & service issues to efficiently increase value for the
business & our customers"
I. Pre-empting: My main function as a Platform Support Associate is to ensure that I actively
monitor the systems we control. With this comes a heavy reliance on data - I need to be able
to identify anomalous data quickly, execute functions and queries at a moment’s notice, and
provide accurate statistics on the quality of a platform's service at any given time. This helps
me detect issues before they are reported by external stakeholders, and the skills taught in
this apprenticeship enable me to perform these actions quicker.
II. Solving: Problem Management is a core component of our ITSM framework. I need the tools,
technical expertise, and confidence to manage product and service issues effectively. The
KSBs taught on this program encourage me to become a SME (Subject Matter Expert) in
many areas of my role.
III. Efficiently: There are many processes I must follow within my role. There are also many
inefficient processes that can be improved. This apprenticeship allows me to provide
expertise in a number of areas that could be automated. My role requires me to be able to
upskill my peers, be a leader, and provide skills that benefit not just myself but others within
my team.

Databases & Organisational Architecture
I use different databases depending on the platform in question. When accessing data, I use an
analytics platform called Looker, supplied by Google Cloud. This operational data is supplied and
managed by a key external stakeholder , who are responsible for the back end processes
and overall database management. The data I use comes from the ad serving infrastructure,
which is ingested into a data warehouse that populates Looker ready for OLAP processing. I can
access and export this operational data in order to conduct analysis. The data I use for is almost
always alpha-numerical, and comes in a pre-defined format when exporting (such as CSV or XLS),
which are both examples of structured data [K5] . Looker is queried using LookML, which builds SQL
2
queries that can evaluate the database, however this is behind a UI that I use to build queries in a
more user friendly experience. Although we are notified of any downtime due to maintenance or
security patching, If I notice any issues with this database, I can escalate these to be troubleshooted
via a Service Desk ticket.
Concerning I primarily work with both RUM (Real User Monitoring) and log level data
through an observability platform called Datadog. RUM data is supplied directly from the end-user’s
session, and I can access supplemental log level data supplied through an API from a serverless AWS
environment. Much of this data is collected in JSON, which is considered to be unstructured due to
its undefined format . However, Datadog has the ability to collect insights on this data that can be
transformed into a structured format. For example, I can build a dashboard that can be downloaded
in various Excel file formats. Furthermore, for data concerning platform usage directly, I can gather
data from internal RDBMS (Relational Database Management System) using AWS Quicksight,
where there are a number of self-service dashboards I can export.
Lastly, data relating to aspects of my core role, such as support tickets, can be pulled directly from
the service desks I use:

Project 1: Resource Planning Dashboard & Forecast
Part A: Historical Ticket Data Dashboard
Situation
As part of future planning, my line manager asked me to collaborate on a resource plan for the team,
looking at our workload across each core workstream. In this first part of the project, I focussed on
providing insights into our historical workload; the leading question being “how has our team’s
workload across all service desks changed over time?”.
In accordance with UK Competition Law, the data used could contain competitor information.
Therefore the results of my analysis are for internal use only; with the principal stakeholder being my
line manager. This satisfies ethical wall policy, ensuring competitor information is not
communicated outside of permitted contexts, which could cause unfair advantages [K2,K15,B1] .
3

times; which indicate how long it took a support agent to begin investigating and finalising an issue
after assignment. Combined with overall ticket volume, this enables me to build a visual timeline of
workload trends.
Action

to collate together. Both and have similar methods of accessing data, however there are

The dashboard in Figure 1.4 above has the potential to become a self-serve tool once implemented,
therefore I paid close attention to the experience of the end user. It is crucial to consider this as the
impact of a visualisation can be lost when design elements are overlooked. Each dashboard uses a
neutral and light colour scheme, using opposing colours on the colour wheel to address colour
blindness. The visualisations themselves also have an off-white background, to make viewing them
less harsh visually. I also ensured that the colour scheme is consistent, using orange, blue and pink to
represent acknowledgement, resolution time, and ticket volume respectively. Lastly, I applied a
6-point moving average to my data, in order to dampen the effects of outliers and better show the
overall trend in acknowledgement/resolution time [K7, S5] .
9
Whilst this dashboard is built using bar charts and line graphs (which could be interpreted as ‘basic’
visualisations), I used this approach to fit the needs of the primary stakeholders - my team. These
insights can be used within our regular meetings, and basic visualisations like these can be easily
digested. They also need to be easily understood by all members of the team, many of whom would
need to verbally interpret the data, but do not have expertise in describing more complex datasets.
Additionally, my line manager expressed an interest in having the ability to drill down on this data, so
to address this I added slicers to the dashboard to allow filtering by agent, date or service desk.
Implementing these slicers allows my line manager (principal stakeholder) to understand the data
beyond top-level insights, further improving the effectiveness of this dashboard [S5, S14] .

Part B: Operational Efficiency Forecast
Situation
As a result of Part A of the resource planning project, my line manager (principal stakeholder)
requested that I investigate future workload trends across our core workstreams. As a result of my
analysis, I would need to build a picture of my team’s probable workload. This would then be
presented to senior stakeholders in order to assess whether a new hire is required for the future
workstreams I am due to begin working on with my team. Therefore, I adapted the leading question
for this part of the project to “how can we use historical data to inform our team’s workload
across all service desks over the next year?”.
Task
Given that I’ve extended the scope of this project from part A, there is no need to access any more
data. I can adapt the existing data I already have for the service desks which will save time on data
cleaning [B7] . Resolution time is the most important insight to stakeholders as it measures how
12
quickly we can fix an issue, so forecasting this metric will provide the most insight.
I plan to create a forecast model similar to the simple forecast conducted in Figure 1.4 of the previous
project, using a more sophisticated modelling technique to provide a forecast that is as accurate as
possible.
Action
I planned to use Python to complete the time series forecast required. Whilst I could have used
Google Sheets; Figure 1.6 demonstrates the limitations of the forecasting options available. Using
Python, I can employ forecasting techniques that account for more options, such as stationarity and
seasonality. Additionally, whilst not all stakeholders are familiar with function, I can adapt the model
using functions and user input, to make them simple to replicate with other datasets in future [S9] .
13
Upon loading the data into Python and beginning data cleaning, I noticed an issue. In Part A of this
project I had converted resolution time data into a duration format (“HH:MM:SS”). However, due to
the method used in Google Sheets, Python recognised this data as string values. Working with
duration in Python is difficult, as the data type should be changed by converting to a time delta.

back to its original format, decimal hours. This
resolved the issue as Python now recognised my
time data as floats, meaning they can be easily

Fig. 1.8 - Output of initial exploratory data analysis for resolution time.
Once I resolved this problem, I began exploratory data analysis. Figure 1.8 shows the actual resolution
time values, plotted against their mean and trend (using NumPy polyfit). It was important to make
note of my observations here, as this would affect the choice of forecast model used. Looking at the
actuals, I observed that the variance in my data appears to remain constant, deducing that my data
was homoscedastic. I was not able to visually identify seasonality, therefore this would require further
exploration. Lastly, comparing the mean and trend lines gave me a good indication that the data is
unlikely to be stationary. This is an important metric for time series analysis, as many forecast models
require stationary data, and thus I may need to de-trend my dataset.
To make a more informed decision on stationarity, I
conducted a hypothesis test. This is a statistical
method that tests a theory using the concept of
statistical significance, to make deductions about
data. Hypothesis testing is crucially important to
data analysis as it defines a statistically correct path
of action. Using Figure 1.8, I can theorise or assume
that my data is not stationary, however the
Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test I conducted in
Figure 1.9 gives me both confidence and evidence
of my hypothesis. Testing my data using a 5% alpha
level, I obtained a value of 0.021. As this is less than 0.05, I concluded that this is a statistically
significant result, and so I do not fail to reject the null hypothesis that my data is not stationary
[K13,S10] .

Now that I had concluded information around the trend, stationarity, and scedasticity of my data, I
began investigating seasonality. Figure 1.10 below shows the seasonal decomposition of resolution
time data using the seasonal period 12, as my data is resampled by month.
Fig. 1.10 - Seasonal decomposition of resolution time data, showing actuals (top-left), trend (bottom-left),
seasonality (top-right) and residuals (bottom-right).
The decomposition confirmed that I can see a negative trend in my data, alongside clear monthly
seasonality. I deduced this using the top-right graph in Figure 1.10, which clearly shows a recurrent
monthly pattern in my data. To conclude my exploratory analysis, I needed to construct a time series
model for non-stationary data, that is able to account for both trend and seasonality.
I decided to construct 2 time series models in order to compare and contrast:
I. Holt’s Linear Forecast: A forecasting method that is able to account for trends in data, but
ignores seasonality.
II. Holt Winter’s Exponential Smoothing (HWES) Forecast: A method that is able to account for
both trend and seasonality in data.
Using the train-test-split method, I allocated the first 80% of my resolution time data into a training
data frame, and the remaining 20% into a testing data frame. Then, using the train and test data I was
able to construct both a Holt’s Linear and HWES forecast, shown below in Figure 1.11 [S13] .

Both of the forecasts above are examples of predictive analytics, where machine learning techniques
are applied to form predictions data - making an educated guess of the future state of my dataset. I
also looked into metrics such as the mean and trendline, both of which are forms of descriptive
analytics. This is the use of summary statistics to describe data - informing the state of a dataset as it
is currently. Lastly, my analysis as part of this project hopes to yield a result with some actionable
insight. This is a form of prescriptive analytics - using modelling to define a course of action, or
prescribing a set of instructions/outcomes to reach a desired goal [K14] .
17
Looking at the forecasts in Figure 1.11, I noticed that the
Holt’s Linear forecast was similar to the forecast
generated in Part A of this project (see Figure 1A.4).
This was due to both forecast methods not accounting
for seasonality, and thus the forecast does not look
visually accurate compared to the test data. In
comparison, the HWES takes into account seasonality
and produces a result not too dissimilar from my test
data, which is the sign of a good forecast model.
To evaluate this further, I compared performance metrics for each forecast type, shown in Figure 1.12.
Both the RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) and MAE (Mean Absolute Error) show the difference
between predicted and actual values, with RMSE being the standard deviation of the difference and
MAE representing the variance. Therefore, a value of 0 in either performance metric would represent
a model that is statistically considered a perfect fit. In this case, the RMSE/MAE values of 0.26 and
0.17 days respectively for the HWES are lower than that of the Holt’s Linear model, indicating that the
HWES is a better fit. Furthermore, there are other performance metrics, such as the AIC (Akaike
Information Criterion) and BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion), that evaluate a model based on the
proximity of values to 0. Once again, as the HWES has closer AIC and BIC values to 0, I can further
conclude that the HWES model is statistically better.
Finally, I refit my data into the HWES model built, as shown below in Figure 1.13. Both the trend and
seasonality considerations are clearly accounted for, and I noted this as a discussion point with
stakeholders. Contextually, I also know that there are plans for my team to stop supporting

Project 2: False Alerting Regression Model
Situation
As one of the senior members on the team, it is my responsibility to manage the service desks that I
work across. Since its launch in October 2022, the FreshService service desk
has been integrated with a number of internal tools. One of these is DataDog, a monitoring
and observation tool which alerts our team about any production issues with the ad platform. As
the platform has become exponentially busier over time, I have seen the number of false alerts
creating tickets in FreshService, which has impacted both my own and the wider team’s productivity.
After discussions with internal stakeholders, I agreed to head a project to analyse the number of alerts
we are receiving, with a view to communicate results to other stakeholders within the department and
advise that alerting thresholds in DataDog should be reviewed. Some initial analysis already exists,
however the insights are weak and I believe that this is insufficient to conclude that we should instruct
other teams to review thresholds they have set up. Therefore, twinned with my hypothesis that
alerting is affected by growing platform usage, I constructed the leading question “Is there a
relationship between the number of false alerts we are receiving and platform usage?”. My
aim was to advise on the need for an alerting review, as this could have significant benefit to my
team’s workload [B1,B5] .
19
The stakeholders involved in this project are:
I. Line Manager: High power, low interest interest internal stakeholder involved in discussions
around the need for this analysis.
II. Engineering Team: Low power, low interest internal stakeholders that I will consult with give
the results of this project.
III. Platform Support Team: My team, our collective input is required to classify false alerts, and
the results of this project impact this team directly.
Task
The data I plan to collect will be across 2 resources:
I. Alert Ticket data exported from FreshService directly.
II. Platform Usage data taken from AWS Quicksight, a BI tool that can access RDBMS
(Relational Database Management System). Due to access restrictions, I cannot construct
SQL queries to collect data but I have access to pre-populated dashboards containing
relevant data [K6] .
20
Once collected, I plan to create a logistic regression model that can predict and classify the
probability of a false alert occurring based on the number of orders submitted in the platform.
20
K6: Described my organisation’s database structure, and how I can access data.
19
B1: Planned to conduct analysis that contributed to improved workplace productivity.

Action
I began with data collection, first exporting a list of orders submitted by day from AWS Quicksight.
This data came from a pre-populated dashboard and was in the form of a CSV file. Then I
downloaded alert data from FreshService. The FreshService UI allows for field customisation,
therefore I was able to export to CSV only the relevant columns (date & basic ticket information)
which saved time with data cleaning. Given the comma delimited format of each dataset, both can
be identified as structured data [K5] .
21
Before I could move on to analysis, there was a small
amount of manual data preparation needed with the
data from FreshService. My aim was to evaluate the
probability of at least 1 false alert occurring, given the
number of orders submitted on that day. As this is a
binary outcome, I decided that a logistic regression
model would work best as this is a classification
problem, rather than evaluating 2 continuous variables using a linear regression model [S9] . So, with
22
my team’s assistance I manually assigned a binary value to each alert, as shown in Figure 2.1. Once this
was complete, I was able to aggregate this in a pivot table by date, and save this as the dataset used
for analysis
I began building my model by loading the data into Python and joining both the order and alerts
datasets into one dataframe, so that they are comparable. I did this using the pandas merge function,
performing an inner join so that only matching values from each dataset remained, shown below in
Figure 2.3 [K10] .
23
Logistic regression models are built off of
linear regression models, therefore I decided
that the best way to truly understand the
outputs would be to build both a linear and
logistic model. To avoid bias in my data, I
made sure to use the test-train-split method.
I assigned 80% of my data to the training
model, ensuring a random and stratified
selection to ensure the train model remains in
proportion to my original dataset.
Before compiling both models, I made time to understand the predictive analysis I am undertaking.
As supervised learning models, both models are only as insightful as the user that constructs them,
and both linear and logistic regression come with a number of benefits and risks. I ensured to take
these into consideration when building and evaluating my model:
23

K5: Identified the format of data collected.
Fig. 2.1 - Assigning binary values to alerts data
Fig. 2.3 - Performing an inner join in Python.
17
Benefits
I. Linear regression models are easy to understand and evaluate; performance metrics such as
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error), MAE (Mean Absolute Error) and R-Squared can be used
to explain the model. Linear regression is also simple to extrapolate beyond the bounds of
the input data, given the model represents its inputs well.
II. Logistic regression models are excellent at classifying data and examining relationships as
probabilities. They also produce more insights than a linear model, as they can measure the
relevance of the independent variable as well as its correlation.
Risks
I. Linear regression models can be very sensitive to outliers, and can significantly affect the
efficiency of a model when there are a smaller number of data points. Linear models also act
under a number of assumptions such as normality (errors are normally distributed) and
homoscedasticity (errors have equal variance). Therefore, extra care should be taken during
exploratory analysis to ensure these assumptions do not fail.
II. Logistic regression models require binary data, and will fail to predict a continuous outcome.
Models can also be prone to overfitting when using a small number of data points, meaning
the model fits the training data too closely and becomes inaccurate for new data [K14] .
24
Taking the above into consideration, I first built a linear regression model based on my training data.
Fig. 2.4 - Linear regression model showing regression line intercept and coefficient (bottom-right),
performance metrics (top-right) and prediction threshold (left)

Figure 2.4 above shows the linear regression model I constructed. The first observation I made was
that it is clear this is not an optimal model for my data. When evaluating the risks I noted that linear
regression acts under the assumption of normality - due to the nature of binary data it is not possible
for my dataset to be normally distributed, therefore I knew this would negatively affect the feasibility
of this model [S11] . Furthermore, when interpreting performance metrics I observed the following:

I. The RMSE value of 0.4578 informally means that the model has an inaccuracy of 45.78%.
Given that the range of orders submitted is between 0-200, I considered this to be a
significant margin of error.
II. The MAE value of 0.4209 informally means that the model has an inaccuracy of 42.09%. This
is a slight improvement in comparison to the RMSE value, however I continued to consider
this as a significant error margin.
III. The R-Squared value for this model is 0.1294, meaning that only 12.94% of the variance in
classification of false alerts is explained by this model. Generally, a high R-Squared value is
considered desirable, therefore I deduced that this model may not be a good fit for my data -
87.06% of the difference in the distribution of false alerts is unexplained by the model. This is
a significant result.
IV. Lastly, the linear regression threshold looks at the independent value that lies on the 50th
percentile of the binary outcome. The value of 37.57 suggests that days where the number of
orders submitted is greater than or equal to 38 are statistically more likely to cause a false
alert.
Given the observations above alongside the evaluation of normality, it was clear to me that this is not
an optimal model, therefore I continued on to build a logistic regression model, which hopefully yields
better results.
Fig. 2.5 - Logistic regression model showing sigmoid curve, accuracy metrics (top-right) and sample
predictions (bottom-right).

S11: Applying considerations with predictive analytics in the context of my data and models chosen.
19
Relating to Figure 2.5 above, although built on a linear regression, the logistic regression uses a
sigmoid curve - a non-linear output. Therefore, I needed to use different performance metrics in
order to assess the feasibility of my model. I made the following observations:
I. The logistic regression threshold of 38.14 was not too dissimilar from the prediction of the
linear regression threshold (37.57). This means the model suggests that days where orders
are over 39 are more likely to produce a false alert. The closeness of the 2 values for logistic
and linear regression likely indicate that the linear regression was heavily affected by outliers in
the data, especially given my deductions from the RMSE and MAE values. I highlighted some
example outliers in green in Figure 2.4 to communicate to stakeholders as part of the results
[S11] .
26
II. The baseline accuracy of 0.6 is based on the maximum value I expect this model to classify
an order submission amount to 1, or producing a false alert. The value suggests that to guess
for each observation that no false alert occurs, I would be correct 60% of the time.
III. The model accuracy value is comparable to the R-Squared value generated from the Linear
Regression model. For the logistic regression model, I got a value of 0.6923, suggesting that
according to the model I constructed in Figure 2.5, it is 69.23% accurate. This is both an
improvement on the Linear Regression model in Figure 2.4, and the baseline accuracy
evaluated above. It also concludes that given the baseline accuracy, this model classifies my
data better than a ‘null guess’.
IV. Contextually, I analysed some test predictions that helped communicate the results to
stakeholders. For example, this model suggests that when 100 orders are submitted, there is
a 23.5% chance that no false alert will be produced, and a 76.5% chance that a false alert
occurs.
Given my evaluation of the performance metrics, the logistic regression model suggests that the
probability of a false alert occurring increases as the number of orders submitted on a given day
increases - predicting that any number of orders submitted per day over 38 are more likely than not
to cause a false alert. Therefore, according to this model there is enough evidence to confirm a
relationship and communicate the results of my analysis based off the leading question constructed
[K13,S10] .

Result
After consulting with stakeholders, the outputs of this analysis were overwhelmingly positive.
Combined with the existing analysis already conducted, I was able to communicate the need for a
prioritised alerting review.
